n: Walk carefully when you go to worship. It is better to come ready to listen and obey than to offer careless sacrifices like fools who don’t realize they are doing wrong.

f.g: Watch your step — approach God with care and reverence.

n: Don’t rush into hasty promises or wordy prayers before God. He is in heaven and we are on earth, so let reverence keep our words few and sincere.
Just as too much busyness produces restless dreams, too many words reveal a fool. Chatter is not the same as devotion.
When you make a promise to God, keep it quickly. God takes no pleasure in people who make vows lightly and then forget them.
It is better not to make a vow at all than to make one and break it. This applies naturally to the covenants we make with God today.
Don’t let your mouth lead you into sin, and don’t excuse a broken vow to the priest by calling it a mistake. Why provoke God to undo the work of your hands?

f.g: Hebrew mal’ak — messenger; likely the temple priest who received vows (compare Malachi 2:7).

n: Many dreams and many words are empty. The answer is simple: revere God.
Don’t be shocked when officials oppress the poor and twist justice. Each official is watched by a higher one — and above all of them is God.

f.g: Each official guards his turf above another; ultimately God sees all.

n: The land’s produce benefits everyone; even a king depends on the fields. Society, high and low, rests on honest farming.

f.w: the king himself is served by the field
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; it may mean a king who cares for the farmland benefits the land.

n: Whoever loves money will never have enough, and whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with more. Greed has no finish line.
As wealth grows, so do the people who consume it. The owner often gets little more than the pleasure of looking at it.
A worker sleeps well whether he eats much or little, but the rich man’s worries keep him awake at night.
The Preacher has seen a painful evil: wealth hoarded by its owner that ends up harming him.

f.g: A grievous wrong or sickening misfortune.

n: Then the riches are lost in a bad venture, and when he has a son there is nothing left to give him.

f.g: An unlucky business deal or misfortune.

n: We are born with nothing and we die with nothing. No earthly possession can be carried out of this life.
It is tragic that a person leaves exactly as he came. What did he gain by working for the wind?
Such a person lives his days in gloom, filled with frustration, sickness, and anger.
The Preacher’s positive counsel: it is good and fitting to enjoy food, drink, and work during the life God gives. That enjoyment is our God-given share.
When God gives someone wealth and also the ability to enjoy it with gratitude, that combination is a true gift from God.
Such a person won’t brood over life’s brevity, because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.

f.g: God keeps him busy (or answers him) with gladness.
